title: Certificate verification is disabled
summary: The endpoint accepts a peer certificate without building and validating a trusted path.
applicable_when: TLS authenticates a remote peer.
check: Inspect verification flags, callbacks, trust configuration, and negative tests.
evidence: A permissive callback, verify-none option, or successful connection with an untrusted certificate.
impact: An active attacker can impersonate the peer and terminate TLS.
remediation: Enable full certificate path validation against an appropriate trust store.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: Reference identity is not verified
summary: A valid certificate for another service name is accepted because hostname or service identity matching is absent.
applicable_when: A client connects to a named TLS service.
check: Trace the expected name into the library identity-verification API and test a mismatched certificate.
evidence: Chain validation succeeds without matching the intended DNS name or other reference identifier.
impact: Any certificate from a trusted issuer may impersonate the target service.
remediation: Perform protocol-appropriate service identity verification using the original reference identity.

references.title: RFC 9525: Service Identity in TLS

title: Identity is matched against the wrong name
summary: Verification uses a redirected host, reverse DNS name, user-controlled Host header, or post-normalized value instead of the original reference identity.
applicable_when: The connection target and asserted application identity can differ.
check: Trace where the reference identifier originates and how redirects and aliases alter it.
evidence: Identity matching against an attacker-influenceable or derived name.
impact: Attackers may redirect trust to a certificate valid for a different identity.
remediation: Bind verification to the application's original, authenticated reference identity.

references.title: RFC 9525: Service Identity in TLS

title: Wildcard certificate matching is overbroad
summary: Wildcard handling spans multiple labels, matches partial labels, or covers a namespace beyond policy.
applicable_when: The verifier supports wildcard DNS identifiers.
check: Test wildcard placement, label count, public suffixes, and IDNA handling.
evidence: Acceptance of names outside the single-label wildcard semantics required by the profile.
impact: A certificate for a broader pattern can impersonate unintended services.
remediation: Use a standards-conformant identity matcher and constrain wildcard issuance/use by policy.

references.title: RFC 9525: Service Identity in TLS

title: Certificate validity period is ignored
summary: NotBefore or NotAfter failures do not reject the path, or validation uses attacker-controlled time.
applicable_when: X.509 certificates establish current peer trust.
check: Inspect validation-time source and test expired and not-yet-valid certificates.
evidence: Successful validation outside the certificate validity interval.
impact: Expired, premature, or compromised credentials remain accepted.
remediation: Use a trustworthy clock and enforce every certificate validity interval.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

title: Basic constraints are not enforced
summary: A non-CA certificate or a path exceeding pathLenConstraint is accepted as an issuer.
applicable_when: Custom certificate path validation or unusual trust anchors are used.
check: Build adversarial chains with CA=false and exceeded path length.
evidence: A leaf or constrained CA successfully signs an accepted subordinate certificate.
impact: Unauthorized certificates can become trust issuers.
remediation: Use a complete path validator that enforces basicConstraints and path length.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

title: Key usage or extended key usage is ignored
summary: A certificate is accepted for signing, TLS server, TLS client, or another purpose it was not authorized to perform.
applicable_when: Certificates contain usage restrictions or serve multiple protocols.
check: Test incompatible keyUsage/EKU combinations at each verification role.
evidence: Acceptance despite absent or conflicting required usage bits/OIDs.
impact: Credentials can be repurposed across roles and protocols.
remediation: Enforce key usage and extended key usage for the exact validation purpose.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

title: Name constraints are not enforced
summary: A constrained CA can issue names outside its permitted namespace and those chains validate.
applicable_when: The chain contains nameConstraints or private PKI subordinates.
check: Test permitted and excluded DNS, IP, email, and directory subtrees.
evidence: An out-of-constraint leaf validates.
impact: A subordinate authority can escape its delegated namespace.
remediation: Use a validator that correctly propagates and enforces name constraints.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

title: Unknown critical certificate extensions are ignored
summary: Validation succeeds when a critical extension is unsupported or malformed.
applicable_when: Certificates may contain critical extensions.
check: Inject or locate an unrecognized critical extension and trace validation.
evidence: Successful path validation while a critical extension is unprocessed.
impact: Security restrictions encoded by issuers can be silently bypassed.
remediation: Reject certificates containing any unrecognized or unprocessable critical extension.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

title: Certificate parser and verifier disagree
summary: Different components canonicalize names, algorithms, lengths, or extensions differently.
applicable_when: More than one X.509 parser or policy component handles the same certificate.
check: Compare raw and parsed values across components using malformed or ambiguous encodings.
evidence: A certificate accepted by one component but interpreted differently by another.
impact: Parser differentials can bypass identity, policy, or revocation decisions.
remediation: Use one strict parser/validator or enforce a canonical representation and consistent policy.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

title: Algorithm parameters in certificates are weak or inconsistent
summary: Signature algorithm identifiers, parameters, or public-key constraints are accepted despite mismatch or policy failure.
applicable_when: Certificate algorithms are parsed from untrusted input.
check: Compare inner/outer signature algorithms, parameter encodings, hashes, and key sizes.
evidence: Mismatched identifiers or disallowed parameters still validate.
impact: Attackers may exploit parser discrepancies or downgrade signature strength.
remediation: Require consistent identifiers and enforce an explicit current algorithm policy.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

title: Revocation requirement fails open
summary: OCSP/CRL lookup errors, stale responses, or responder failures silently convert to trusted status where policy requires revocation checking.
applicable_when: The trust policy requires revocation status.
check: Exercise revoked, unknown, stale, unreachable, and invalidly signed responses.
evidence: A policy-required revocation check fails yet the connection succeeds.
impact: Known-compromised certificates remain usable.
remediation: Define fail behavior explicitly, validate freshness/signatures, and use stapling or operational alternatives suited to availability needs.

references.title: RFC 6960: Online Certificate Status Protocol

title: Pinned credential cannot rotate safely
summary: Pinning accepts only one expiring key/certificate without backup or update path, encouraging disabled verification during incidents.
applicable_when: The application pins certificates or public keys.
check: Inspect backup pins, update authorization, expiry, and recovery behavior.
evidence: A single immutable pin or an update path that bypasses normal trust.
impact: Operational failure can cause outages or emergency trust bypasses.
remediation: Pin only with a managed rotation and recovery design, and retain normal identity validation where appropriate.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: SSLv2 or SSLv3 is negotiable
summary: The endpoint can negotiate obsolete SSL protocol versions.
applicable_when: The TLS stack exposes legacy protocol configuration.
check: Probe minimum/maximum versions and all listener configurations.
evidence: A successful SSLv2 or SSLv3 handshake.
impact: Known protocol and cipher weaknesses can remove confidentiality and integrity.
remediation: Disable SSLv2 and SSLv3 in every endpoint and shared policy.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 is negotiable
summary: The endpoint permits deprecated TLS versions.
applicable_when: TLS protects live application traffic.
check: Probe all endpoints and fallback paths for TLS 1.0/1.1.
evidence: A completed handshake using TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1.
impact: Legacy constructions and downgrade exposure weaken transport security.
remediation: Set the minimum to TLS 1.2 and prefer TLS 1.3.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: Protocol downgrade protection is incomplete
summary: Version fallback, middlebox compatibility, or custom negotiation can select a weaker protocol without detection.
applicable_when: More than one protocol version or transport mode is available.
check: Manipulate negotiation and fallback signals and inspect downgrade sentinels/transcript binding.
evidence: A weaker version succeeds after attacker-induced failure without authenticated downgrade detection.
impact: An active attacker can force weaker security than both peers support.
remediation: Use standard downgrade protections, disable ad hoc fallback, and authenticate negotiation.

references.title: RFC 8446: TLS 1.3

title: Weak or deprecated cipher suite is enabled
summary: The configuration permits NULL, export, RC4, 3DES, static RSA, anonymous, or otherwise disallowed suites.
applicable_when: TLS 1.2 or earlier exposes configurable suites.
check: Enumerate offered and accepted suites from every endpoint role.
evidence: Handshake success with a suite prohibited by current policy.
impact: Traffic may lack authentication, forward secrecy, or adequate cryptographic strength.
remediation: Use a narrow current suite policy centered on AEAD and ephemeral key exchange.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: CBC suite lacks encrypt-then-MAC
summary: TLS 1.2 CBC records use MAC-then-encrypt without successfully negotiating encrypt_then_mac.
applicable_when: A CBC cipher suite remains enabled for TLS 1.2.
check: Inspect extension negotiation and test record error/timing behavior.
evidence: CBC handshake without encrypt_then_mac or distinguishable record failures.
impact: Padding-oracle and timing attacks may disclose plaintext.
remediation: Disable CBC suites or require encrypt_then_mac where legacy CBC is unavoidable.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: TLS 1.2 GCM nonce can repeat
summary: The explicit nonce construction is random, resettable, or shared unsafely rather than uniquely tied to record sequence.
applicable_when: TLS 1.2 AES-GCM is implemented or wrapped by custom record code.
check: Trace nonce construction across reconnect, resume, process restart, and concurrency.
evidence: Repeated nonce under a traffic key or a construction without a uniqueness guarantee.
impact: GCM confidentiality and authenticity can fail catastrophically.
remediation: Construct nonces from the record sequence as recommended and enforce per-key limits.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: Per-key record or byte limits are not enforced
summary: A traffic key protects more records/data than the AEAD security bound permits.
applicable_when: High-volume or long-lived TLS/DTLS sessions are possible.
check: Inspect counters, key update triggers, and behavior near limits.
evidence: No key-update/reconnect path or counters that wrap/continue past policy.
impact: Forgery or confidentiality advantage grows beyond the intended bound.
remediation: Track usage per traffic key and update keys or terminate before the applicable limit.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate is mishandled
summary: Peers ignore, race, indefinitely defer, or desynchronize requested traffic-key updates.
applicable_when: TLS 1.3 supports long-lived connections or explicit KeyUpdate.
check: Exercise bidirectional updates during concurrency and near record limits.
evidence: Continued old-key use, counter reset, deadlock, or cross-direction confusion.
impact: Key limits may be exceeded or records processed under the wrong epoch.
remediation: Use the library state machine correctly and test concurrent update transitions.

references.title: RFC 8446: TLS 1.3

title: Forward secrecy is absent
summary: Static RSA, static DH, PSK-only resumption, or long-lived ticket keys allow later compromise to decrypt recorded sessions.
applicable_when: The threat model includes retrospective compromise.
check: Inspect negotiated key exchange and resumption modes plus ticket-key rotation.
evidence: Sessions established without an ephemeral contribution where forward secrecy is required.
impact: A later long-term-key compromise exposes previously captured traffic.
remediation: Prefer ephemeral (EC)DHE and psk_dhe_ke resumption; rotate ticket protection keys.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: DH or EC group is too weak or unapproved
summary: The endpoint accepts small finite-field parameters, curves below policy strength, or arbitrary explicit groups.
applicable_when: TLS 1.2 permits configurable groups or custom DH parameters.
check: Enumerate supported groups and validate DH parameter generation and sizes.
evidence: Handshake success with a group below current policy or attacker-selected explicit parameters.
impact: Discrete-log attacks or invalid-group behavior can reveal session secrets.
remediation: Restrict negotiation to current approved named groups and adequate finite-field sizes.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: Handshake signature uses MD5 or SHA-1
summary: TLS authentication accepts deprecated signature hashes.
applicable_when: TLS 1.2 or legacy certificate/signature paths remain available.
check: Enumerate signature algorithms and test certificate and handshake selection.
evidence: A completed handshake authenticated with MD5 or SHA-1.
impact: Collision weaknesses undermine authentication guarantees.
remediation: Disable deprecated signature algorithms and use SHA-256 or stronger current schemes.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: Compression or related plaintext-length oracle is enabled
summary: TLS-level or application-adjacent compression combines attacker-controlled and secret plaintext under observable encryption.
applicable_when: Secrets and attacker input share compressed encrypted contexts.
check: Inspect TLS compression and higher-layer response compression around secrets.
evidence: Negotiated compression or measurable size changes correlated with secret guesses.
impact: Adaptive length observations can recover secret plaintext.
remediation: Disable TLS compression and separate secrets from attacker-controlled compressed contexts.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: Renegotiation is insecure or unexpectedly enabled
summary: Legacy renegotiation lacks secure binding or application state is not bound across renegotiation.
applicable_when: TLS 1.2 or earlier permits renegotiation.
check: Probe secure renegotiation indication and application authorization transitions.
evidence: Unbound renegotiation or privilege/state carried across a new handshake incorrectly.
impact: Attackers may splice handshakes or confuse authentication state.
remediation: Disable renegotiation unless required; require secure renegotiation and reset/bind application state.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: TLS 1.3 0-RTT performs replay-sensitive actions
summary: Early data triggers non-idempotent, authorization-changing, or financially significant operations without replay defense.
applicable_when: TLS 1.3 early data is accepted.
check: Replay captured early data across connections, regions, and ticket lifetime.
evidence: Repeated side effects or authorization decisions from one early-data flight.
impact: Attackers can duplicate valid actions without breaking TLS.
remediation: Disable 0-RTT or restrict it to explicitly replay-safe operations with application-level defenses.

references.title: RFC 8446: TLS 1.3

title: Session ticket protection is weak or long-lived
summary: Tickets are plaintext, unauthenticated, protected by shared static keys, or accepted beyond their intended lifetime.
applicable_when: Stateless TLS resumption is enabled.
check: Inspect ticket encryption/authentication, key scope, rotation, lifetime, and multi-node distribution.
evidence: Readable/malleable tickets or a long-lived widely shared ticket key.
impact: Attackers may forge sessions, recover state, track clients, or negate forward secrecy.
remediation: Use authenticated ticket protection, narrow key scope, frequent rotation, and bounded lifetimes.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: Resumption bypasses current authentication or policy
summary: A resumed session retains identity, authorization, cipher, or certificate assumptions that are no longer valid.
applicable_when: Sessions can resume after policy, credential, or account state changes.
check: Revoke/change policy and attempt resumption across deployment nodes.
evidence: Successful resumption with stale authorization or unacceptable parameters.
impact: Revoked users or obsolete security policy remain effective.
remediation: Bind resumable state to policy version and identity lifecycle; force full handshake when assumptions change.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: ALPN or protocol selection is not bound to handling
summary: The negotiated application protocol differs from the parser/router actually used or can be omitted ambiguously.
applicable_when: One TLS endpoint serves multiple application protocols.
check: Trace ALPN offer/selection into dispatch and test missing/unexpected values.
evidence: Traffic parsed under a protocol not explicitly and consistently negotiated.
impact: Cross-protocol messages may bypass authentication or parser assumptions.
remediation: Require an allowed ALPN value and bind it to one unambiguous handler.

references.title: RFC 8446: TLS 1.3

title: SNI influences trust or routing without binding
summary: An unauthenticated or mismatched SNI selects tenant, certificate, backend, or authorization state inconsistently with verified identity.
applicable_when: Virtual hosting or tenant routing uses SNI.
check: Compare SNI, certificate identity, HTTP authority, and backend selection under mismatches.
evidence: A request reaches or authenticates to a tenant inconsistent with verified names.
impact: Tenant confusion can expose data or credentials across virtual hosts.
remediation: Define and enforce consistent binding among SNI, verified certificate identity, and application authority.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: Mutual TLS identity is not mapped safely to authorization
summary: Possessing any trusted client certificate grants access, or ambiguous subject fields determine the account.
applicable_when: Client certificates authenticate users, devices, or services.
check: Trace validated certificate identifiers through account mapping and authorization.
evidence: Broad trust-store acceptance, subject-string parsing, or missing EKU/policy checks.
impact: A certificate valid for another purpose or principal gains unintended access.
remediation: Map stable constrained identifiers after full client-auth validation and apply explicit authorization.

references.title: RFC 5280: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile

title: Plaintext fallback remains reachable
summary: Connection errors, certificate failures, or feature negotiation cause the application to retry without TLS.
applicable_when: The application supports both secure and insecure transports.
check: Induce TLS and validation failures and observe retry paths.
evidence: Successful operation over plaintext after a TLS-related failure.
impact: An active attacker can strip transport protection.
remediation: Remove plaintext fallback or require an authenticated, explicit policy transition.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: TLS errors expose distinguishable cryptographic states
summary: Alert choice, timing, retry, or application response reveals padding, tag, certificate, or handshake-secret validity beyond protocol requirements.
applicable_when: Attackers can submit malformed records or handshakes repeatedly.
check: Cluster timing and responses for controlled invalid inputs.
evidence: Stable distinctions correlated with secret-dependent validation stages.
impact: Adaptive attackers may turn implementation behavior into decryption or authentication oracles.
remediation: Use hardened library paths, minimize externally visible distinctions, and avoid application processing after failure.

references.title: RFC 8446: TLS 1.3

title: Private keys or session secrets are logged
summary: Debugging, key-log callbacks, crash diagnostics, or observability export TLS private material in production.
applicable_when: TLS diagnostics or instrumentation is present.
check: Search key-log environment variables, callbacks, logs, dumps, and support bundles.
evidence: Recoverable traffic secrets, premaster secrets, PSKs, or private keys in diagnostic output.
impact: Anyone with the logs can decrypt captured traffic or impersonate endpoints.
remediation: Disable secret logging in production and treat necessary diagnostic captures as highly sensitive and short-lived.

references.title: RFC 8446: TLS 1.3

title: Certificate and cipher policy differs across equivalent endpoints
summary: Nodes, regions, IPv4/IPv6 listeners, or fallback services expose materially weaker TLS configurations.
applicable_when: Multiple endpoints serve the same security identity.
check: Enumerate every address, region, CDN/backend path, and protocol listener.
evidence: One equivalent endpoint negotiates weaker versions, suites, groups, or validation.
impact: Attackers can redirect clients to the weakest deployment member.
remediation: Apply and continuously test one centrally governed TLS policy across all equivalent endpoints.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS

title: DTLS replay window or epoch handling is incorrect
summary: Duplicate records are accepted, replay state resets, or records from old epochs are processed after key transitions.
applicable_when: DTLS protects datagram traffic.
check: Replay, reorder, duplicate, and delay records across epoch/key changes.
evidence: Repeated application effects or acceptance outside the defined replay window/epoch.
impact: Attackers can duplicate authenticated actions or confuse record state.
remediation: Implement and persist the DTLS replay window and epoch transitions exactly as specified.

references.title: RFC 9325: Secure Use of TLS and DTLS
